caption:
The US approved licenses for about 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for Chinese companies, a House committee revealed.
Tencent alone was cleared for 150,000. Companies had asked for 3.4 million.
Nvidia says it has since stopped shipping H200s to China.

Should the US sell its best AI chips to China at all?

site_article.headline: House committee says US approved about 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China
site_article.dek: Documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee show Commerce licensed H200 and MI325X sales to Chinese firms, including companies on a Pentagon list.
site_article.summary: The House Foreign Affairs Committee disclosed on November 19, 2026, that the Commerce Department approved licenses for about 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026. Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million chips in that period.
site_article.seo_title: US approved 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China
site_article.seo_description: A House committee says Commerce approved about 879,000 Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X chips for Chinese firms such as Tencent, out of 3.4 million requested.
site_article.answer_summary: According to documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Commerce Department approved licenses for about 879,000 advanced AI chips from Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026. Nvidia says it has since stopped shipping H200 chips to China.
site_article.hero_alt: News photo used by Reuters to illustrate a report on US AI chip sales to China.

paragraphs.text: The US Commerce Department approved licenses for about 879,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to be sold to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, according to documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee on November 19, 2026, Reuters reported. The chips covered are Nvidia's H200 and AMD's comparable MI325X.

Companies had sought permission to ship about 3.4 million of the chips to China over the same period, according to the committee's figures as reported by Reuters and by CNBC, whose report was summarized by PrimeXBT News. Reuters noted that it was not immediately clear how many of the approvals led to actual shipments.

The approvals included 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for the carmaker BYD, Reuters reported. All four appear on the Pentagon's list of companies it alleges are backed by the Chinese military.

Committee chair Brian Mast released the license information using his authority under the Export Control Reform Act, according to a committee statement cited by Reuters. Members voted at a committee meeting to release the documents, according to the CNBC report as summarized by PrimeXBT News.

Mast also said two firms named in Nvidia license applications, Maginfra and New Matrix, are suspected fronts for smuggling. "Both are fake companies," he said at the meeting, according to the same report, and he described any approvals to them as a serious concern. Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the committee, said the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security had failed to enforce the rules and called for rigorous oversight by Congress.

Nvidia said the approvals were subject to strict conditions and limited volumes, and that despite receiving some licenses it has since stopped shipping H200 chips to China, Reuters reported. AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters, and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CNBC.

Lawmakers from both parties have called for legislation that would impose stricter controls on sales of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries, according to the CNBC report as summarized by PrimeXBT News.

The figures show how far the licensing pipeline went before shipments stalled. Approvals of this size for some of China's largest technology groups give lawmakers who want Congress to have a say over chip export licenses a concrete number to point to, even though actual deliveries appear to have been far smaller than the approvals.

The next signal is whether the House advances legislation that gives Congress a role in AI chip export licenses, and whether Commerce explains the approvals to the two firms Mast described as suspected fronts.
